source.title: GEM: Geometric Entropy Mixing for Optimal LLM Data Curation
source.authors: Yue Min; Ziyun Qiao; Rui Chen; Yu-Jun Li

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports a downstream-performance sweep over training-token budgets, which bears on V6, but it does not measure held-out pretraining-loss power laws or fit scaling exponents.
record.gate_note: The main experiments compare data-mixing strategies at a fixed 1.1B parameters and 25B tokens; they do not test scaling laws or compute-optimal allocation. The pilot study varies token budget and reports downstream-performance trends, so only those results are included as rows. The RegMix validation-loss predictability experiment concerns mixture weights, not scaling runs.
record.test_reason: This is a data-mixing method paper at a fixed 1.1B parameters and 25B tokens. It cites Kaplan et al. but measures no loss-versus-scale relationship, fits no law and makes no prediction. The only scale-varying result is a pilot in Appendix H.2, described as validating the training configuration. It covers one unspecified downscaled setup over a 5x token range (5B, 10B, 15B, 25B). It reports downstream accuracy with no fitted or predicted trend, so it cannot show whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale (V6). The paper's statement that GEM mixtures 'consistently yield superior scaling laws' is not backed by any scaling measurement.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that GEM's hyperspherical, balance-regularized clustering yields better data categorization and improves downstream accuracy (by up to about 1.2%) across DoReMi, Perf and RegMix at 1.1B parameters and 25B tokens. They also say it gives more predictable mixing, measured by RegMix Spearman correlation on validation loss across mixtures. They call the 1.1B/25B setting an early-stage indicator needing larger-scale validation. The token pilot is framed as confirming optimization stability, not as a scaling-law result.
record.recipe_differences: This study evaluates a data-curation and mixing method; it does not use the original scaling-law measurement or fitting recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: In the token-budget pilot, Logic & Linguistics plateaus relatively early while Science QA and Commonsense Reasoning show steady gains.

fits_no_version.finding: In a downscaled pilot (parameter count unstated), average downstream accuracy rises from 41.05% to 42.12% as tokens go from 5B to 25B. The category scores dip at 15B and Logic & Linguistics plateaus after 10B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A single small-run token sweep of downstream accuracy, used as a training sanity check rather than a scaling-law test.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The scaling-related pilot uses a downscaled setup whose parameter count is not stated, covers only 5B–25B tokens, reports downstream accuracy rather than pretraining loss, and provides no fitted law or uncertainty estimates. Several category-level values are figure-only.
record.rows_left_out: No additional scaling-law results are reported. Main comparisons change data categorization or mixture strategy at fixed model size and token budget, so they do not bear on the claim versions.

untested.parts: Predictability of downstream performance from scale or loss: no fit, no extrapolation, narrow single-setup range.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' classification and its V6 supports/limits_scope labels are not justified. The pilot cannot test predictability, and the figure's values contradict 'steady gains' for Science QA and Commonsense. The pilot's 25B average (42.1) matches the GEM average in the Fig. 6 ablation, so the 'downscaled' model may be the main setup; this is unclear. The RegMix predictability probe concerns mixture weights, not scale.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute; power-law behavior and its range.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocations and their trends with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities and training regimes, including repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer.
The pilot reports downstream accuracy over token budgets, but does not test predictions from pretraining loss, fit a predictive relationship, or test runs across several orders of magnitude.
Dependence of scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices, and departures from a single power law.

rows.value: 42.12% at 25B tokens; the text describes improvement as consistent and monotonic
rows.note: The paper reports the endpoint values and monotonic trend in text; it does not provide a fitted predictive law.
rows.check: The average rises monotonically (41.0, 41.4, 41.6, 42.1 per Fig. 8), but this is one sanity-check trajectory. There is no fit or prediction, the parameter count is unstated, and it is unclear whether these are separate runs or checkpoints, so it cannot show predictability as V6 names it.
